commits.messageBody:
Some Dang invocations took 5 to 7 seconds longer than their work, at the
very end, once everything was already done.

Each invocation serves the module a private API over a loopback
listener, runs the function, then shuts that server down. The function's
GraphQL client used the process-wide http.DefaultTransport. Under
concurrent requests that pool can dial a connection that never carries a
request: request A holds the only connection, B starts a dial, A finishes
first, B takes A's connection, and B's dial completes with nothing to do.
The server sees that connection in StateNew, and http.Server.Shutdown
only counts StateNew as idle after 5 seconds. So the invocation waited
out that grace period for a connection nobody used.

Give each invocation its own transport and close its idle connections
right before Shutdown. Requests still in flight are drained as before;
only the connections with nothing on them go away at once.

It shows up most on `dagger generate`, whose functions fire many calls
concurrently. On a Rust module, edit + generate over 8 runs: two runs
stalled, 6.1s and 16.5s, against a 2.0s median; with the drain, max 2.6s
and no stall. Medians do not move; the tail does.

Verify:
  go test -race -count=3 -run TestServeNestedClient ./core/sdk/dang/shared
  The first test builds the stray connection deliberately and fails in
  5.3s without the drain, passes in 10ms with it.
Signed-off-by: Guillaume de Rouville <guillaume@dagger.io>
commits.messageHeadline: fix(dang): drain the nested client's connection pool before shutdown

commits.messageBody:
When you are logged in to Dagger Cloud, every command ended by uploading
a metrics report with nothing in it.

The CLI exports three things to Cloud at exit: traces, logs and metrics.
The OpenTelemetry metrics reader always performs one last collection
when it shuts down, whether or not anything was ever recorded. Most CLI
commands record no metrics at all, so that final collection is an empty
ResourceMetrics, and the exporter dutifully POSTed it to Cloud: one full
round trip, in the exit path, for a request that carries nothing.

Skip a collection that has no instrumentation scopes, before it takes a
sequence number. A collection with real data, an explicit empty scope,
errors, flush and shutdown all behave as before; the only request that
disappears is the one with no contents.

Measured on a cached `dagger check` while logged in, three instrumented
runs: the meter provider's shutdown went from 73-81ms to 0. Cloud
telemetry shutdown is 205-325ms in total on this machine; what remains
is the final trace upload, which does carry data.

Not logged in: nothing changes, there is no Cloud exporter to skip.

Verify:
  go test -race -run 'Test(SequencedMetrics|ExportSequenc)' ./engine/telemetry
Signed-off-by: Guillaume de Rouville <guillaume@dagger.io>
commits.messageHeadline: perf(telemetry): skip the empty Cloud metrics upload on shutdown

commits.messageBody:
Every schema build in the engine JSON-encoded the whole schema and hashed
it, to have a digest ready in case something asked for one. Only the
schema-scoped cache inputs ever ask; query validation does not. A
command builds several schemas, one per served module and nested client,
so most of that encoding was for digests nobody read.

Keep the digest as a sync.OnceValue created alongside the schema, and
have SchemaDigest fetch both under the same lock, so an install between
"build" and "read digest" can no longer yield a stale or empty digest.
The digest is still computed exactly once per schema; just not before
someone wants it.

Engine CPU during a loop of cached `dagger check` commands, engines from
main with and without this change, 25s pprof each:

    dagql schema building, share of engine CPU   7.6%  -> 4.6%
    per cached check                             34ms  -> 21ms of engine CPU

That is CPU inside the engine, not wall time. On the command itself the
difference sits inside the noise of a 700ms check; the original
measurement had -25ms median on 4 of 5 pairs, which I could not resolve
again on today's machine.

Verify: go test -race -count=3 -run 'TestSchemaDigest|TestImplicitInputCachePer|TestViews' ./dagql
Signed-off-by: Guillaume de Rouville <guillaume@dagger.io>
commits.messageHeadline: perf(dagql): compute the schema digest lazily

commits.messageBody:
…d of syncing directories

Loading a local module synced three directories from your machine before
doing any work, each time only to read one small file or to learn whether
one exists.

The engine already has two ways to talk to the machine that ran the
command. Uploads through host.directory and host.file bring data in as an
input, content-addressed and cached: right for a module's source tree.
Plain session requests, ReadCallerHostFile and StatCallerHostPath, answer
a question about the host: right for find-up, and how the workspace
config is already read. The module loader used the first kind for three
questions: the module config's bytes, whether the module directory holds
a .env, and whether a .env found up the tree is a regular file. Each was
a filesync round trip, a client walk and a snapshot, 15 to 30ms apiece.

Use the second kind for the three questions. The context directory, the
module's real input, still goes through host.directory with its
content-addressed reuse, and it includes the config file, so the module's
implementation digest still follows config changes.

Nothing behaves differently. The config read was already noCache, the
probes were once-per-session calls, a module directory that does not
exist yet (dagger init) still yields no inner .env, a .env that is a
directory or a symlink is still ignored, and a .env that exists is still
read through host.file and asEnvFile.

The cost being avoided really belongs to the upload tier: host.file
could fast-path a single file with no directory snapshot, and
Directory.exists on a one-name include could answer from a stat. That
would make this change unnecessary and help every module that reads a
host file the plain way. Not done here.

Measured on a cached `dagger check` with a local Dang module, engines
built from main with and without this change, client timeline:
Query.moduleSource 73ms -> 34ms; whole command about 25ms faster over 10
interleaved pairs, the rest being noise around a 700ms command.

Verify:
  go test ./core/integration -run 'TestWorkspaceCompat/TestOuterEnvFile|TestEnvFile|TestModuleLoading/TestModuleSourceResolution'
Signed-off-by: Guillaume de Rouville <guillaume@dagger.io>
